plan.angle: Title: 'What Is Petrelintide? The Amylin Weight-Loss Shot Explained' (OK). Credit the source as 'The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, published online around 30 Sep 2026 (Zealand release, 30 Sep 2026)'; confirm the exact online date on the paper. Headline number: '9.0 mg petrelintide, the trial's highest arm: about 10.7% average weight loss at 42 weeks versus 1.7% on placebo (efficacy estimand; 10.2% treatment-policy)', with per-arm n from the paper. Nausea line: 'Across all petrelintide doses combined, 20% had nausea (79 of 404) versus 6% on placebo.' Say vomiting and GI discontinuations are zero only 'at the highest dose, per Zealand'. Status line: 'Investigational. Not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of 25 Oct 2026. Zealand and Roche say a Phase 3 programme (ZUPREME) has started.' Give dates only from ClinicalTrials.gov or company releases (e.g. ZUPREME-2, NCT06926842). Keep 'smaller than tirzepatide's in separate trials, not head-to-head'. Keep pramlintide label wording without doses. Keep the prescriber line, 'not personal advice' and 'don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own'.

plan.why: Tests the playbook's under-covered pipeline-drug hypothesis behind EloraTZP (499). The name is new, competition is low, mainstream press picked it up on Oct 24, and a peer-reviewed paper plus settled amylin physiology give the depth a long-form needs to pass the fact-check. | fact-check: The topic is valid and fits the pipeline-explainer test. Checked against the Zealand release on BioSpace (Sep 30, 2026), the Lancet D&E abstract record PIIS2213-8587(26)00213-5 and press coverage. Three things in the plan need fixing. (1) Date: the paper was published around Sep 30, 2026, alongside EASD 2026, not in October. (2) Status: Zealand and Roche say a global Phase 3 ZUPREME programme 'has been initiated', so 'Phase 2' on its own is out of date. (3) Nausea: 19.6% (79 of 404) is pooled across all five petrelintide doses (1.0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.0 and 9.0 mg). Placebo is 5 people (6%, consistent with 6.2%, but confirm the placebo n from the paper). The 10.7% is the 9.0 mg arm against 1.7% on placebo at week 42 under the efficacy estimand. Under the treatment-policy estimand it's 10.2%; state both. The release reports 485 adults analysed (493 enrolled), mean BMI 36.7, mean age 47, 53% female. Per-arm n must come from the paper. The Lancet page returned 403 to the fetcher, so the scriptwriter must confirm per-arm n and the population wording from the paper itself. The 'no vomiting and no GI discontinuations' claim applies only 'at the maximally effective dose' (Zealand wording); keep that scope. The watch-next video is already published, so naming it is fine, but don't echo its 'beat' frame in L1's own narration. Petrelintide is not a GLP-1 drug: the series name is fine, but say so out loud. Don't name dose strengths as advice; trial arm labels only.

package.description:
Watch next: How Long Does Tirzepatide Take to Work? Week by Week in the Trials https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XqT9kLmP3Rw

What is petrelintide? An investigational weekly shot that copies amylin, a pancreatic hormone, not GLP-1.
Phase 2 ZUPREME-1 (485 adults with overweight or obesity), best-performing dose: up to about 10.7% average weight loss at 42 weeks vs 1.7% on placebo if people stay on treatment (up to 10.2% vs 1.4% counting everyone). Nausea: about 20% across all doses (79 of 404) vs about 6% on placebo.
As of 25 October 2026 it is not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA; Zealand said on 29 September 2026 a global Phase 3 programme has been initiated.

This is general information, not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you, and please don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. Anything sold online as "petrelintide" is not an approved medicine.

Sources:
1. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, ZUPREME 1, 29 Sep 2026: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/landia/article/PIIS2213-8587(26)00213-5/abstract

script.working_title: What Is Petrelintide? The Amylin Weight-Loss Shot Explained
script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' scenario + counterintuitive claim ("a new weekly weight-loss shot that isn't a GLP-1 drug at all"), first concrete answer by about 15 s, and an open loop ("one number that may matter more than the weight loss") paid off in the side-effects chapter

scenes.section: What is petrelintide?
scenes.narration: It's eleven at night. You're scrolling, and a headline says there's a new weekly weight-loss shot that isn't a GLP-1 drug at all. Your first thought might be: wait, is that even real?

visual.stock_query: curious person scrolling phone in bed

scenes.retention_device: Pattern interrupt: relatable late-night moment plus a counterintuitive claim

scenes.section: What is petrelintide?
scenes.narration: It is. It's called petrelintide, and it copies amylin, a hormone your pancreas releases alongside insulin. In its Phase 2 trial, the best-performing dose averaged up to about ten point seven percent weight loss at forty-two weeks, versus one point seven percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Best-performing petrelintide dose, average loss, week 42

scenes.retention_device: Immediate concrete answer to the hook

scenes.section: What is petrelintide?
scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you'll know what amylin actually does, how it differs from GLP-1, what that trial really found, and whether you can get it. Spoiler on that last one: not yet.
scenes.on_screen_text: What you'll know by the end
scenes.retention_device: Explicit promise of what the viewer gets

scenes.section: What is petrelintide?
scenes.narration: And there's one number from that trial that might matter more to you than the weight loss itself. We'll get there, along with the asterisk most headlines left out.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in the side-effects chapter

scenes.section: What is petrelintide?
scenes.narration: Picture someone like Dana, a hypothetical forty-seven-year-old. She's heard about Ozempic and Mounjaro, and she's also heard the nausea stories. So when she sees the word 'amylin', her question is simple: is this gentler, or just newer?

visual.stock_query: thoughtful woman reading news at kitchen table

scenes.section: What is petrelintide?
scenes.narration: If you've wondered the same thing, that's a completely fair question. Let's answer it honestly, with the evidence.

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: So first: what is amylin?

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: Here's the twist. Amylin wasn't discovered as an appetite hormone. In nineteen eighty-seven, researchers found it inside clumps of protein, called amyloid, in the pancreases of people with type two diabetes.

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: That's where its scientific name comes from: islet amyloid polypeptide. But it turned out to be much more than a clump. Amylin is released by the same beta cells that make insulin, together with it, when you eat.

visual.stock_query: two hormone buddies leaving pancreas together

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: So what does it do? Three main things. It slows how fast your stomach empties. It helps hold back glucagon, a hormone that raises blood sugar, after meals. And it helps tell your brain you've had enough.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, answered as a list

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: That brain signal lands partly in a small area of the brainstem called the area postrema. It's one of the few spots where the brain can sample the blood directly, so it picks up hormones like amylin quickly.

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: Think of insulin and amylin as a two-person team after every meal. Insulin moves the sugar where it needs to go. Amylin gently closes the kitchen door.

visual.stock_query: cartoon hormone gently closing kitchen door

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: So if amylin already does all this, why did it take almost forty years to turn it into a weekly shot? The answer is surprisingly physical.
scenes.on_screen_text: Why did it take so long?

visual.stock_query: puzzled Medi looking at calendar pages

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: Human amylin is sticky. In solution, it tends to clump into fibres, the very kind of clumps it was discovered in. That makes the natural hormone a tricky starting point for a medicine.

visual.stock_query: sticky molecules clumping in a vial

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'why so long' loop

scenes.section: What is amylin?
scenes.narration: So chemists rebuild it. Petrelintide is an engineered, long-acting amylin analogue from Zealand Pharma, designed to be injected just once a week.
scenes.retention_device: Resolution that bridges to the next chapter

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Now, the question Dana really cares about. How is this different from GLP-1?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change tied to the hypothetical thread

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: A lot of headlines lump every new weight-loss shot together as 'another GLP-1'. This one isn't. Petrelintide mimics a different hormone, made in a different place, using a different receptor.

visual.myth: Every new weight-loss shot is a GLP-1
visual.fact: Petrelintide mimics amylin, a separate hormone

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: GLP-1 comes mostly from cells lining your gut. When food arrives, it boosts insulin, but mainly when blood sugar is raised. It also slows the stomach and quiets appetite through the brain.

visual.stock_query: friendly gut cells waving at food

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Your own GLP-1 lasts only about two minutes before an enzyme breaks it down. That's why medicines like semaglutide and tirzepatide are engineered to last a whole week.

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Amylin, by contrast, comes from the pancreas. And it docks onto a different receptor: a calcitonin receptor teamed up with helper proteins called RAMPs.

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: So, side by side: a different source and a different receptor, but overlapping effects. Both slow the stomach, and both nudge you toward feeling full sooner.

visual.stock_query: two roads meeting at one town

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: But here's where it gets interesting. Because they work through different pathways, scientists think the two might add together. So one of the biggest ideas in this field isn't amylin instead of GLP-1. It's amylin plus GLP-1.

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: Petrelintide isn't the only amylin drug, either. Novo Nordisk has its own, called cagrilintide, which was tested in a Phase 2 weight trial published in twenty twenty-one.

visual.stock_query: two amylin molecules on lab shelf

scenes.section: Amylin vs GLP-1: what's the difference?
scenes.narration: And Roche, which partnered with Zealand on petrelintide in March twenty twenty-five, said it plans to develop it both on its own and in combination with Roche's own incretin drug, called C T three eight eight.

scenes.section: Is amylin new? The pramlintide story
scenes.narration: Is amylin even new as a medicine? Not quite.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change with a teaser answer

scenes.section: Is amylin new? The pramlintide story
scenes.narration: Back in twenty oh-five, the FDA approved pramlintide, sold as Symlin, the first amylin-based medicine.

scenes.section: Is amylin new? The pramlintide story
scenes.narration: But it's a very different tool. Its label covers people with type one or type two diabetes who use mealtime insulin and still haven't reached their glucose goals. It's injected with meals, not once a week, and it isn't approved for weight loss.

visual.stock_query: dinner plate with clock beside it

scenes.section: Is amylin new? The pramlintide story
scenes.narration: Its most common side effect is nausea, and it carries a boxed warning about severe low blood sugar when used with insulin.

scenes.section: Is amylin new? The pramlintide story
scenes.narration: So pramlintide showed that amylin biology works in people. What it didn't offer was a simple weekly shot built for weight. That's the gap petrelintide is trying to fill.

visual.stock_query: missing puzzle piece shaped like calendar

scenes.section: Is amylin new? The pramlintide story
scenes.narration: Which brings us to the big question. Did a weekly amylin shot actually deliver? Let's look closely, because two of the headline numbers look almost identical and mean different things.

visual.stock_query: two lookalike numbers side by side

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: So, what did the petrelintide trial actually show?

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: The trial is called ZUPREME one, a placebo-controlled Phase 2 study. Zealand first shared topline results on the fifth of March, twenty twenty-six, and the full paper was published in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology on the twenty-ninth of September, twenty twenty-six.

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: Zealand's topline counted four hundred and ninety-three people, and the published paper reports four hundred and eighty-five adults with overweight or obesity randomly assigned. On average, they were forty-seven, with a BMI of thirty-six point seven, and fifty-three percent were women.

visual.stat_label: adults randomised in the published paper, ZUPREME-1

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: People living with type two diabetes were studied separately, in a trial called ZUPREME two. Zealand reported its first results on the seventh of October, twenty twenty-six: up to nine point two percent weight loss at twenty-eight weeks, versus two point zero percent on placebo, in two hundred and twenty people.
scenes.on_screen_text: ZUPREME-2 (type 2 diabetes): up to 9.2% vs 2.0%, week 28, per Zealand
scenes.retention_device: Fresh dated fact that prevents a wrong takeaway

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: Back to ZUPREME one. Participants were split into six groups: five petrelintide dose arms or placebo, given as a weekly shot for forty-two weeks.

visual.stock_query: six colourful groups on a calendar

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: Phase 2 trials like this one are mainly about finding the right dose and spotting safety signals. They're smaller and shorter than the trials regulators usually rely on for approval.

visual.stock_query: Medi adjusting dial on a machine

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: In the best-performing dose arm, average weight loss at week forty-two was up to about ten point seven percent of body weight. On placebo, it was one point seven percent.

visual.stat_label: Best dose arm vs 1.7% placebo, week 42
visual.stock_query: bar chart with tall blue bar

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: Now, the first asterisk. That ten point seven percent uses what's called the efficacy estimand. In plain English: what happens if people stay on treatment as planned.

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: There's a stricter way to count, called the treatment-policy estimand. It includes everyone, whether they stopped the shot early or not. Counted that way, weight loss was up to ten point two percent, versus one point four percent on placebo.

visual.stock_query: everyone counted on a tally board

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions. The stricter one is closer to real life, where not everyone stays on a treatment.

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: For someone weighing two hundred pounds, ten percent is about twenty pounds. That's roughly a large bag of dog food, gone over nearly ten months.

visual.stock_query: happy person lifting bag of dog food

scenes.section: What did the petrelintide trial show?
scenes.narration: Is that a lot? It depends what you compare it to, and that's where headlines get sloppy. We'll get to the comparison. But first, the number I promised you at the start.

visual.stock_query: curtain about to open on stage

scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: new loop plus signalling the main payoff

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: Remember Dana's worry? For many people starting GLP-1-type medicines, stomach side effects like nausea are among the most common, especially in the early weeks.

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: Across all petrelintide doses combined, about twenty percent had nausea: seventy-nine of four hundred and four people. On placebo, it was about six percent.
scenes.retention_device: Main loop payoff: the number that may matter more

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: And in the trial's maximally effective dose arm, there was no vomiting, and nobody stopped treatment because of stomach side effects.
scenes.on_screen_text: Top dose arm: no vomiting, no GI dropouts

visual.stock_query: calm stomach character giving thumbs up

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: Here's the second asterisk. That twenty percent is pooled. It mixes lower doses with higher ones, so it isn't the nausea rate at any single dose.

visual.stock_query: different coloured marbles in one jar

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: And the no-vomiting result comes from one dose arm, in one Phase 2 trial. It's encouraging, but it needs to hold up in bigger, longer studies.

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: So no, this isn't a side-effect-free shot. Nausea still happened about three times as often as on placebo. It just looks less common than many people might expect.

visual.myth: Amylin shots have no side effects

scenes.section: Petrelintide side effects: how common is nausea?
scenes.narration: Which raises the obvious question: less common than what? Time for the comparison everyone wants to make, done properly.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: question bridges to next chapter

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: Petrelintide versus tirzepatide: can you even compare them?

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: Tirzepatide's big obesity trial, SURMOUNT one, enrolled two thousand five hundred and thirty-nine adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes.

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: On the fifteen milligram dose, average weight loss was twenty point nine percent at seventy-two weeks, versus three point one percent on placebo.

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: Nausea on that fifteen milligram dose: thirty-one point zero percent, versus nine point five percent on placebo. Diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation were also common.

visual.stock_query: stomach character looking queasy but okay

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: So, counting everyone in both trials, petrelintide's weight loss was smaller than tirzepatide's, about ten percent versus about twenty-one, in separate trials, not head-to-head. Its pooled nausea rate looks lower, with the same caveat.

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: And those trials differ in almost every way: different people, forty-two weeks versus seventy-two, different counting methods, and a mid-stage trial versus a large late-stage one. No trial has compared them directly.
scenes.on_screen_text: Why it's not a fair fight

visual.stock_query: apples and oranges on a scale

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: So the honest takeaway isn't 'which one wins'. It's that amylin may offer a different trade-off, and maybe, one day, a partner for GLP-1-type drugs rather than a rival.

visual.stock_query: two characters teaming up high five

scenes.section: Petrelintide vs tirzepatide: can you compare?
scenes.narration: For Dana, that's genuinely useful. The amylin story isn't about replacing what already works. It's about more options down the road, for different bodies and different tolerances.

scenes.narration: So, is petrelintide approved, and when could it come out?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter change; pays off the promise from the opening

scenes.section: Is petrelintide approved? When could it come out?
scenes.narration: Here's the status as of the twenty-fifth of October, twenty twenty-six. Petrelintide is investigational. It is not approved by the FDA, the MHRA, Health Canada or Australia's TGA.

scenes.section: Is petrelintide approved? When could it come out?
scenes.narration: On the twenty-ninth of September, twenty twenty-six, Zealand said a global Phase 3 ZUPREME programme has been initiated. Phase 3 is the large, late-stage testing that usually comes before any approval decision.

scenes.section: Is petrelintide approved? When could it come out?
scenes.narration: There's no confirmed approval date. And anything sold online as 'petrelintide' right now is not an approved medicine. If you're interested, the safe route is asking a prescriber about approved options, or about clinical trials.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask a prescriber about approved options

scenes.section: Is petrelintide approved? When could it come out?
scenes.narration: Meanwhile, there are big questions this trial can't answer yet. Three of them matter most.

visual.stock_query: three question marks on a shelf

scenes.section: Is petrelintide approved? When could it come out?
scenes.narration: Does the weight loss keep going beyond forty-two weeks? How much of the weight lost is fat versus muscle? And what happens when amylin is paired with a GLP-1-type drug? Larger and combination studies are where those answers will come from.
scenes.retention_device: Honest uncertainty, payoff of the numbered loop

scenes.narration: Let's pull it all together.

factcheck.summary: All the numbers and study descriptions check out against primary or near-primary sources. ZUPREME-1: 485 randomised (493 at topline), age 47, BMI 36.7, 53% women, 5 doses plus placebo over 42 weeks; weight loss up to 10.7% vs 1.7% (efficacy estimand) and 10.2% vs 1.4% (treatment-policy estimand); nausea 79/404 (20%) vs 5/81 (6%); no vomiting and no stomach-related stopping at the maximally effective dose; Lancet D&E 29 Sep 2026; topline 5 Mar 2026; Phase 3 'has been initiated' per Zealand. ZUPREME-2 (7 Oct 2026): 220 people, up to 9.2% vs 2.0% at week 28. The Roche CT-388 plan, SURMOUNT-1 figures (2,539; 20.9% vs 3.1%; nausea 31.0% vs 9.5%), the Symlin 2005 label and the amylin/GLP-1 biology are all correct. Framing is careful: the tirzepatide comparison is labelled indirect, Phase 2 limits are explained, status is dated, there's an anti-gray-market line, and the disclaimer and prescriber line are both present. Four minor wording fixes are listed. Note: the Lancet page and the GlobeNewswire release returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch. Their content was confirmed through search results, a syndicated copy of the release and press reports quoting the paper.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean, on-brand (purple/blue palette, logo, short headlines ≤4 words effectively) and legible at phone size. #0 'MEET AMYLIN' wins on CTR: it pairs a genuinely expressive, labelled character (surprised stomach/gut mascot) with a curiosity gap that directly serves the title's promise ('isn't GLP-1' → so what is it? → a different hormone), without repeating the title's words. The subtext is small but secondary; the big yellow 'AMYLIN' plus the character's startled expression is the real hook and reads instantly even at 168px. #1's red circle highlighting what looks like blank space is a legibility/trust problem (reads as a mistake) and the bare 10.7% stat doesn't match the 'what is this hormone' curiosity the title promises, so it risks pulling in the wrong audience or just looking generic. #2 is the cleanest and most legible, but it drops the emotional/character element the playbook calls for (one labelled character plus one honest emotion) in favor of a fairly generic silhouette-plus-question-mark mystery trope, giving it less emotional pull than #0. Net: #0 offers the best mix of curiosity, emotion and honest payoff tied to the title, with legibility comfortably above the 7 bar.

What is petrelintide? An investigational weekly shot copying amylin, a pancreatic hormone, not GLP-1.
